title: Optimize frequency with a balanced overall design rather than maximizing clock speed
decision: POWER4 was designed around an overall performance objective rather than pursuing the highest possible clock frequency as an isolated goal.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against treating maximum clock frequency as the sole or dominant optimization target.
rationale: The design team considered the interaction between clock frequency, pipeline structure, cache/memory latency, interconnect delays, and overall system performance; a higher frequency was not necessarily worthwhile if it imposed costly trade-offs elsewhere.
outcome: POWER4 achieved a high operating frequency while using a microarchitecture and system organization intended to balance frequency against other sources of performance.

title: Use distributed reliability features instead of relying on a narrow centralized RAS mechanism
where_in_paper: Guiding principles / reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS)
decision: RAS was treated as a system-wide architectural requirement and incorporated throughout the processor, cache, interconnect, and service infrastructure.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper contrasts the pervasive RAS approach with treating reliability primarily as an external or localized support function.
rationale: POWER4 was intended for enterprise-class systems, so faults had to be detected, isolated, and in many cases recovered with minimal impact on continued operation; the architecture therefore incorporated extensive detection and recovery mechanisms.
outcome: The paper reports a processor/system architecture with substantial hardware support for error detection, fault isolation, recovery, and serviceability.

title: Adopt a high-bandwidth distributed interconnect rather than a conventional centralized bus
decision: POWER4 used a distributed, packet-based interconnect architecture to connect processor cores, caches, memory, and I/O-related elements instead of relying on a conventional shared bus.
alternatives_or_rejected: A centralized shared-bus organization was unsuitable for the bandwidth, latency, scalability, and concurrency goals of the system.
rationale: The interconnect had to support multiple simultaneous transactions and the bandwidth demands created by multiple processor cores and large cache structures without making the bus a serialization bottleneck.
outcome: The resulting POWER4 system used a high-bandwidth fabric/interconnect with distributed communication among major system components.

title: Integrate two POWER4 cores on one chip and share major system resources
decision: The implementation placed two superscalar POWER4 processor cores on a single chip and organized the chip around shared cache and interconnect resources.
alternatives_or_rejected: A design using only one core per chip or less tightly integrated resources would not provide the same aggregate throughput and system-level efficiency.
rationale: Integration of multiple cores and shared resources increased computational throughput while reducing the cost and communication overhead of connecting separate processor chips.
outcome: POWER4 was implemented as a two-core processor chip with shared system resources and on-chip communication.

title: Use a large shared L2 cache organization to support the two processors
decision: The two processor cores were organized around a shared large on-chip L2 cache rather than giving each core only an entirely private second-level cache.
alternatives_or_rejected: A purely private L2 organization would complicate sharing and coherence behavior and could duplicate capacity needed by workloads running across the two cores.
rationale: A shared cache allows the two processors to access a common pool of cache capacity and facilitates efficient communication and data sharing between them.
outcome: POWER4 incorporated a large shared L2 cache serving the two cores as a central element of the chip's memory hierarchy.
